authoredSolutions.1: A charge \(q\) of mass \(m\) accelerated from rest through a potential difference \(V\) acquires kinetic energy \(qV\), so its momentum is \(p=\sqrt{2mqV}\) and \[\lambda=\frac{h}{p}=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt{mq}}.\] With \(V\) the same for all three, only the product \(mq\) matters. Taking \(m_{e}\) and \(e\) as units, \(mq=1\) for the electron, \(mq\approx 1836\) for the proton and \(mq\approx 7294\times 2=14588\) for the \(\alpha\)-particle. Since \(\lambda\) falls as \(mq\) grows, \[\lambda_{e^{-}}>\lambda_{p^{+}}>\lambda_{\alpha},\] which is the standard result \(\lambda_{e}=1.227/\sqrt{V}\) Angstrom, \(\lambda_{p}=0.286/\sqrt{V}\) Angstrom, \(\lambda_{\alpha}=0.101/\sqrt{V}\) Angstrom. Hence the correct choice is A. [Source note: the printed stem for this question is a verbatim duplicate of another question in the same file, so the original wording is not recoverable. The stem shown here was reconstructed from the four printed options, which compare the de Broglie wavelengths of an electron, a proton and an alpha particle. The ordering is robust to the exact condition: whether the three are accelerated through the same potential difference, given the same kinetic energy, or given the same speed, the result is the same.]
authoredSolutions.2: The gravitational force on the earth is central, so the angular momentum of the earth about the sun is conserved. Speed is greatest at perihelion (distance \(r_{\min}\)) and least at aphelion (distance \(r_{\max}\)); at both of these turning points the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so \[m\,v_{\max}\,r_{\min}=m\,v_{\min}\,r_{\max}.\] Therefore \[v_{\max}=\frac{r_{\max}\,v_{\min}}{r_{\min}},\] and the correct choice is C. This is exactly Kepler's law of equal areas written for the two apsides.
authoredSolutions.3: For the carrier \(c(t)=4\sin(2\pi\times 10^{7}t)\) the carrier frequency is \(f_{c}=10^{7}\) Hz, and for the message \(m(t)=2\sin(2\pi\times 10^{5}t)\) the modulating frequency is \(f_{m}=10^{5}\) Hz. Amplitude modulation produces two sidebands, \[f_{\text{USB}}=f_{c}+f_{m},\qquad f_{\text{LSB}}=f_{c}-f_{m},\] so the bandwidth of the broadcast signal is \[\Delta f=f_{\text{USB}}-f_{\text{LSB}}=\left(f_{c}+f_{m}\right)-\left(f_{c}-f_{m}\right)=2f_{m}.\] The carrier frequency cancels and only the modulating frequency survives: \[\Delta f=2\times 10^{5}\ \text{Hz}=0.2\ \text{MHz}.\] Hence the correct choice is A.
authoredSolutions.4: A wall can only exert a force along its normal, so only the normal component of the ball's momentum is reversed; the tangential component is unchanged. For normal incidence with speed \(v\), the normal component is \(v\) and \[|\Delta p|_{1}=mv-\left(-mv\right)=2mv.\] For incidence at \(45^{\circ}\) to the normal the normal component is \(v\cos 45^{\circ}\), so \[|\Delta p|_{2}=2mv\cos 45^{\circ}=\frac{2mv}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}\,mv.\] The ratio of the impulses is \[\frac{|\Delta p|_{1}}{|\Delta p|_{2}}=\frac{2mv}{\sqrt{2}\,mv}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{1}.\] Hence the correct choice is B.
authoredSolutions.5: The permittivity varies along \(x\), the direction from one plate to the other, so the slab behaves as an infinite set of elementary capacitors in SERIES. An element of thickness \(dx\) has capacitance \(dC=\varepsilon(x)A/dx\), so \[\frac{1}{C}=\int_{0}^{d}\frac{dx}{\varepsilon(x)A}=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_{0}A}\left[\int_{0}^{d/2}\frac{dx}{1+\frac{kx}{d}}+\int_{d/2}^{d}\frac{dx}{1+\frac{k(d-x)}{d}}\right].\] For the first integral put \(u=1+kx/d\), giving \(\frac{d}{k}\ln\left(1+\frac{k}{2}\right)\); by the symmetry \(x\to d-x\) the second integral is identical. Hence \[\frac{1}{C}=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_{0}A}\cdot\frac{2d}{k}\ln\left(1+\frac{k}{2}\right),\qquad C=\frac{k\varepsilon_{0}A}{2d\,\ln\left(1+\frac{k}{2}\right)}.\] The intended option is B, which carries the factor \(\frac{k\varepsilon_{0}A}{2d}\) together with \(\ln\left(1+\frac{k}{2}\right)\); the correct choice is B.
authoredSolutions.6: Only gravity does work on the bob, so mechanical energy is conserved. Rising through an angle \(\theta=60^{\circ}\) from the lowest point raises the particle by \(h=L\left(1-\cos\theta\right)\): \[\frac{1}{2}mu^{2}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+mgL\left(1-\cos 60^{\circ}\right).\] With \(L=0.5\) m, \(u=3\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) and \(1-\cos 60^{\circ}=\tfrac{1}{2}\), \[v^{2}=u^{2}-gL=9-\left(10\right)\left(0.5\right)=4,\] so \(v=2\ \text{m/s}\) (taking \(g=9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}\) gives \(v=\sqrt{4.1}\approx 2.02\ \text{m/s}\), the same option). Hence the correct choice is D.
authoredSolutions.7: Number of nuclei in \(2\) mg of gold (molar mass \(197\ \text{g mol}^{-1}\)): \[N=\frac{2\times 10^{-3}}{197}\times 6.022\times 10^{23}=6.11\times 10^{18}.\] The decay constant for a half-life of 3 days is \[\lambda=\frac{0.693}{T_{1/2}}=\frac{0.693}{3\times 24\times 3600}=2.67\times 10^{-6}\ \text{s}^{-1}.\] The activity is \[R=\lambda N=\left(2.67\times 10^{-6}\right)\left(6.11\times 10^{18}\right)=1.63\times 10^{13}\ \text{Bq}.\] Converting with \(1\ \text{Ci}=3.7\times 10^{10}\ \text{Bq}\), \[R=\frac{1.63\times 10^{13}}{3.7\times 10^{10}}\approx 441\ \text{curie}.\] Hence the correct choice is C.
authoredSolutions.8: Springs in series add their compliances, so \[k_{eq}=\frac{k\cdot 4k}{k+4k}=\frac{4k}{5}=0.8k=0.8\times 20=16\ \text{N/m}.\] A two-body spring oscillator vibrates about its centre of mass with the reduced mass \[\mu=\frac{m_{1}m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}=\frac{0.2\times 0.8}{0.2+0.8}=0.16\ \text{kg}.\] Therefore \[\omega=\sqrt{\frac{k_{eq}}{\mu}}=\sqrt{\frac{16}{0.16}}=\sqrt{100}=10\ \text{rad/s}.\] Hence the correct choice is A.
authoredSolutions.9: Resolve each set into components (Column II reads \(1=A\), \(2=\) Zero, \(3=2A\), \(4=2\sqrt{2}A\)). Row (R): the vectors are \(A\) along \(+y\), \(A\) along \(+x\) and \(\sqrt{2}A\) at \(45^{\circ}\) between them, so the sum is \(\left(0,A\right)+\left(A,0\right)+\left(A,A\right)=\left(2A,2A\right)\) of magnitude \(2\sqrt{2}A\), giving \(R\rightarrow 4\). Row (S): the vectors are \(\sqrt{2}A\) along \(+y\), \(A\) at \(15^{\circ}\) above \(+x\) and \(A\) at \(45^{\circ}\) below the negative \(x\)-axis, i.e. at \(225^{\circ}\). The components are \[x:\ A\cos 15^{\circ}+A\cos 225^{\circ}=A\left(0.9659-0.7071\right)=0.2588A,\] \[y:\ \sqrt{2}A+A\sin 15^{\circ}+A\sin 225^{\circ}=A\left(1.4142+0.2588-0.7071\right)=0.9659A,\] so the magnitude is \(A\sqrt{0.2588^{2}+0.9659^{2}}=A\), giving \(S\rightarrow 1\). Only options B and D carry both \(R\rightarrow 4\) and \(S\rightarrow 1\). Row (Q) contains \(\sqrt{2}A\) at \(45^{\circ}\) and \(A\) along \(+x\), whose partial sum is already \(\left(2A,A\right)\); no single vertical vector can cancel this, so \(Q\) cannot be Zero and option D is eliminated. The vertical arrow of magnitude \(A\) directed downwards gives \(\left(2A,A\right)+\left(0,-A\right)=\left(2A,0\right)\), i.e. \(2A\), so \(Q\rightarrow 3\) and the two equal and opposite \(\sqrt{2}A\) vectors of row (P) cancel to leave Zero, \(P\rightarrow 2\). Hence the correct choice is B.
authoredSolutions.10: Differentiating \(\vec{r}=10\alpha t^{2}\hat{i}+\left(5\beta t-5\right)\hat{j}\) gives \[\vec{v}=20\alpha t\,\hat{i}+5\beta\,\hat{j}.\] The angular momentum about the origin is \(\vec{L}=m\left(\vec{r}\times\vec{v}\right)\), whose only component is along \(\hat{k}\): \[\frac{L_{z}}{m}=\left(10\alpha t^{2}\right)\left(5\beta\right)-\left(5\beta t-5\right)\left(20\alpha t\right)=50\alpha\beta t^{2}-100\alpha\beta t^{2}+100\alpha t.\] Setting this to zero, \[\alpha t\left(100-50\beta t\right)=0\ \Rightarrow\ t=\frac{100}{50\beta}=\frac{2}{\beta}\] (rejecting the trivial \(t=0\)). Hence the correct choice is C.
authoredSolutions.11: Each wire has the same length \(L\) and the same cross-section \(A\), and joined end to end they carry the SAME tension \(F\) while their extensions add. Using \(\Delta L=FL/\left(AY\right)\), \[\Delta L_{\text{total}}=\frac{FL}{AY_{1}}+\frac{FL}{AY_{2}}.\] The combination has total length \(2L\), so its equivalent modulus satisfies \(\Delta L_{\text{total}}=F\left(2L\right)/\left(AY_{eq}\right)\): \[\frac{2}{Y_{eq}}=\frac{1}{Y_{1}}+\frac{1}{Y_{2}}\ \Rightarrow\ Y_{eq}=\frac{2Y_{1}Y_{2}}{Y_{1}+Y_{2}}.\] The equivalent modulus is the harmonic mean of the two. Hence the correct choice is C.
authoredSolutions.12: With \(N=N_{0}e^{-\lambda t}\), a quarter decayed means three quarters remain: \[\frac{3N_{0}}{4}=N_{0}e^{-\lambda T_{1}}\ \Rightarrow\ T_{1}=\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln\frac{4}{3},\] and half decayed means half remains: \[\frac{N_{0}}{2}=N_{0}e^{-\lambda T_{2}}\ \Rightarrow\ T_{2}=\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln 2.\] Subtracting, \[T_{2}-T_{1}=\frac{1}{\lambda}\left(\ln 2-\ln\frac{4}{3}\right)=\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln\left(\frac{2\times 3}{4}\right)=\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln\left(\frac{3}{2}\right).\] The result is positive, as it must be since \(T_{2}>T_{1}\). Hence the correct choice is A.
authoredSolutions.13: At its rating the bulb draws \[I=\frac{P}{V}=\frac{200}{100}=2\ \text{A},\qquad R_{\text{bulb}}=\frac{V}{I}=\frac{100}{2}=50\ \Omega.\] To dissipate the same power the bulb must carry the same current \(2\) A, so with a series resistance \(R\) on the \(200\) V supply \[\frac{200}{R_{\text{bulb}}+R}=2\ \Rightarrow\ R_{\text{bulb}}+R=100\ \Omega.\] Therefore \(R=100-50=50\ \Omega\). Hence the correct choice is B.
authoredSolutions.14: Every drop starts from rest, so a drop that has been falling for a time \(t\) has fallen \(s=\tfrac{1}{2}gt^{2}\). The observed drop has fallen for \(4\) s: \[s_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\left(9.8\right)\left(4\right)^{2}=78.4\ \text{m}.\] The next drop is \(34.3\) m behind it, so it has fallen \[s_{2}=78.4-34.3=44.1\ \text{m}.\] Its time of fall is \[t_{2}=\sqrt{\frac{2s_{2}}{g}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\times 44.1}{9.8}}=\sqrt{9}=3\ \text{s}.\] The two drops therefore left the tap \(4-3=1\) s apart, i.e. the tap releases \(1\) drop per second. Hence the correct choice is B.
authoredSolutions.15: The wire resistance is \(0.1\ \Omega/\text{cm}=10\ \Omega/\text{m}\), so the full \(10\) m wire has \(R_{\text{wire}}=100\ \Omega\). The steady current from the driver cell is \[I=\frac{6}{20+100}=\frac{6}{120}=0.05\ \text{A}.\] The balancing length \(5.5\) m has resistance \(5.5\times 10=55\ \Omega\), and at balance the unknown cell draws no current, so its emf equals the potential drop across that length: \[E=I\,R'=0.05\times 55=2.75\ \text{V}.\] Hence the correct choice is A.
authoredSolutions.16: The parent nucleus is at rest, so the total momentum before the disintegration is zero and must remain zero: \[0=\vec{p}_{1}+\vec{p}_{2}\ \Rightarrow\ \left|\vec{p}_{1}\right|=\left|\vec{p}_{2}\right|.\] The de Broglie wavelength depends only on the magnitude of the momentum, \(\lambda=h/p\), so \[\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}}=\frac{h/p_{1}}{h/p_{2}}=\frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}=1.\] The ratio is \(1:1\) whatever the mass split, so the unequal masses \(m\) and \(3m\) are irrelevant. Hence the correct choice is D.
authoredSolutions.17: The fringe width is \(\beta=\lambda D/d\), and here \(d=d_{0}+A\sin\omega t\) oscillates between \(d_{0}-A\) and \(d_{0}+A\). Since \(\beta\) varies inversely with \(d\), the widest fringes occur at the smallest separation: \[\beta_{\max}=\frac{\lambda D}{d_{0}-A},\qquad \beta_{\min}=\frac{\lambda D}{d_{0}+A}.\] Subtracting, \[\beta_{\max}-\beta_{\min}=\lambda D\left[\frac{1}{d_{0}-A}-\frac{1}{d_{0}+A}\right]=\lambda D\cdot\frac{2A}{d_{0}^{2}-A^{2}}=\frac{2\lambda AD}{d_{0}^{2}-A^{2}}.\] Hence the correct choice is B.
authoredSolutions.18: Both samples are supplied heat at the same rate, so the heat delivered in a time \(t\) is \(Q\propto t\). From \(Q=mS\,\Delta T\), \[S=\frac{Q}{m\,\Delta T}\propto\frac{t}{\Delta T},\] i.e. the substance whose temperature climbs more slowly has the larger specific heat. From the graphs, substance \(A\) reaches \(120^{\circ}\) in \(3\) s, a rate of \(40\ ^{\circ}/\text{s}\), while substance \(B\) reaches only \(90^{\circ}\) in \(6\) s, a rate of \(15\ ^{\circ}/\text{s}\). Since \(B\) heats more slowly, \[S_{B}>S_{A}.\] (The flat portions that follow are the phase changes, during which the temperature is constant.) Hence the correct choice is B.
authoredSolutions.19: For a uniform disc of mass \(m\) and radius \(R\), the moments of inertia about a diameter and about the perpendicular central axis are \[I_{x}=I_{y}=\frac{mR^{2}}{4},\qquad I_{z}=\frac{mR^{2}}{2},\] the last following from the perpendicular-axis theorem. Since \(K=\sqrt{I/m}\), \[K_{x}=K_{y}=\frac{R}{2},\qquad K_{z}=\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}},\] so \(K_{z}\neq K_{x}\) and the Assertion is FALSE. The Reason is true: \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) are all axes of symmetry of a uniform disc. With a false assertion and a true reason, the correct choice is D.
authoredSolutions.20: The first ball retains one quarter of its speed, so \(v_{1}=\tfrac{1}{4}\times 4=1\ \text{m/s}\). For an elastic collision the relative velocity of separation equals the relative velocity of approach: \[v_{2}-v_{1}=u_{1}-u_{2}=4\ \Rightarrow\ v_{2}=5\ \text{m/s}.\] Momentum conservation then fixes the second mass: \[2\times 4=2\times 1+m_{2}\times 5\ \Rightarrow\ m_{2}=\frac{6}{5}=1.2\ \text{kg}.\] The centre of mass moves with a constant velocity given by the total momentum divided by the total mass: \[v_{cm}=\frac{m_{1}u_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}=\frac{2\times 4}{2+1.2}=\frac{8}{3.2}=\frac{5}{2}\ \text{m/s}.\] Hence the correct choice is C.
authoredSolutions.21: Mayer's relation \(C_{P}-C_{V}=R\) holds exactly only for an IDEAL gas, so a measured value of \(1.1R\) signals a departure from ideal behaviour. For a real (van der Waals) gas the intermolecular attraction gives, to first order, \[C_{P}-C_{V}=R\left[1+\frac{2a}{RTV}\right],\] which always exceeds \(R\) and grows as the temperature falls. The gas therefore behaves ideally, \(C_{P}-C_{V}\to R\), only at high temperature, while the enlarged value \(1.1R\) belongs to the lower temperature. Since \(R\) is measured at \(T=P\) and \(1.1R\) at \(T=Q\), \[T_{P}>T_{Q}\quad\text{i.e.}\quad P>Q.\] Hence the correct choice is B.
authoredSolutions.46: Let \(I=\int_{\pi/24}^{5\pi/24}\frac{dx}{1+\sqrt[3]{\tan 2x}}\). With limits summing to \(\frac{\pi}{4}\), apply \(x\to\frac{\pi}{4}-x\): \(\tan\big(2(\frac{\pi}{4}-x)\big)=\cot 2x\), so the integrand becomes \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{\tan 2x}}{1+\sqrt[3]{\tan 2x}}\). Adding the two forms, \(2I=\int_{\pi/24}^{5\pi/24}dx=\frac{4\pi}{24}=\frac{\pi}{6}\), so \(I=\frac{\pi}{12}\).
authoredSolutions.47: Vertex is \(2\) from the origin and focus \(4\) from it (collinear), so \(a=2\) and the parabola is \(y^2=8(x-2)\). In \(Y^2=8X\) with \(X=x-2\), the origin gives \(X_1=-2,\,Y_1=0\), so \(S_1=Y_1^2-8X_1=16\). The area of the triangle formed by the pair of tangents and the chord of contact is \(\frac{S_1^{3/2}}{2a}=\frac{16^{3/2}}{4}=\frac{64}{4}=16\).
authoredSolutions.48: From \(e^2=\tfrac13\), \(b^2=\tfrac{2}{3}a^2\); the point \((\sqrt{3/2},1)\) then gives \(a^2=3,\,b^2=2\). So \(c=1\), focus \((1,0)\), and the circle is \((x-1)^2+y^2=\tfrac43\). Using \(y^2=2-\tfrac{2x^2}{3}\) yields \(x^2-6x+5=0\Rightarrow x=1\) (\(x=5\) rejected). The intersection points are \((1,\pm\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3})\), so the squared distance between them is \(\big(\tfrac{4}{\sqrt3}\big)^2=\tfrac{16}{3}\).
authoredSolutions.49: \((p\to q)\land(q\to\sim p)=(\sim p\lor q)\land(\sim q\lor\sim p)\). Factoring out \(\sim p\) gives \(\sim p\lor(q\land\sim q)=\sim p\lor F=\sim p\).
authoredSolutions.50: Grouping, \(\sin x+\sin 4x+\sin 2x+\sin 3x=4\sin\tfrac{5x}{2}\cos x\cos\tfrac{x}{2}=0\). In \([0,2\pi]\): \(\sin\tfrac{5x}{2}=0\) gives \(0,\tfrac{2\pi}{5},\tfrac{4\pi}{5},\tfrac{6\pi}{5},\tfrac{8\pi}{5},2\pi\) (sum \(6\pi\)); \(\cos x=0\) gives \(\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\) (sum \(2\pi\)); \(\cos\tfrac{x}{2}=0\) gives \(\pi\). All distinct, so the total is \(9\pi\).
authoredSolutions.52: Expand each term \(\frac{1}{a-kb}=\frac1a\big(1+\frac{kb}{a}+\frac{k^2b^2}{a^2}+\cdots\big)\), dropping \((b/a)^3\) and higher. The \(k^2\) part sums to \(\frac{b^2}{a^3}\cdot\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\), whose leading \(n^2\)-coefficient is \(\frac{b^2}{3a^3}\).
authoredSolutions.53: The middle coefficient of \((1+x)^{20}\) is \(A=\binom{20}{10}\); the two middle coefficients of \((1+x)^{19}\) are \(B=\binom{19}{9},\,C=\binom{19}{10}\). By Pascal's rule \(B+C=\binom{20}{10}\), so \(\frac{A}{B+C}=1\).
authoredSolutions.56: Let \(J=\begin{bmatrix}0&i\\ i&0\end{bmatrix}\); then \(J^2=-I\) and \(J^4=I\). \(J^nM=M\) for all \(M\) requires \(J^n=I\), i.e. \(4\mid n\). The two-digit multiples of \(4\) are \(12,16,\dots,96\), a count of \(\frac{96-12}{4}+1=22\).
authoredSolutions.57: The base is \(1+\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{4k-2}{3^k}=1+2=3\). The exponent is \(\log_{1/4}\!\big(\frac{1/3}{1-1/3}\big)=\log_{1/4}\tfrac12=\tfrac12\). Hence \(l=3^{1/2}\) and \(l^2=3\).
authoredSolutions.58: Simplify \(\frac{x+1}{x^{2/3}-x^{1/3}+1}=x^{1/3}+1\) and \(\frac{x-1}{x+\sqrt x}=1-x^{-1/2}\), so the bracket is \(x^{1/3}+x^{-1/2}\). The general term of \((x^{1/3}+x^{-1/2})^{10}\) is independent of \(x\) when \(\frac{10-r}{3}-\frac r2=0\Rightarrow r=4\); that term is \(\binom{10}{4}=210\).
authoredSolutions.60: \(\vec r\parallel(\vec p+\vec q)\times(\vec p-\vec q)\). With \(\vec p+\vec q=(5,3,2)\) and \(\vec p-\vec q=(1,1,0)\), the cross product is \((-2,2,2)\), magnitude \(2\sqrt3\); the unit vector is \(\frac{(-1,1,1)}{\sqrt3}\). Since \(|\vec r|=\sqrt3\), \(\vec r=\pm(-1,1,1)\) and \(|a|+|b|+|c|=3\).
authoredSolutions.62: As \(x\to2^-\), \([x]=1\) so \(x-[x]\to1\) and \(\tan(x-2)\to0\), giving \(e^0=1\); continuity forces \(\mu=1\). As \(x\to2^+\), \(x^2-5x+6<0\), so \(\frac{|x^2-5x+6|}{-x^2+5x-6}=1\) and the RHL is \(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\). Setting it equal to \(\mu\) gives \(\lambda=\mu^2=1\), so \(\mu+\lambda=2\).

stemOverrides.16: A nucleus of mass \(4\text{ }m\) disintegrates into two daughter nuclei of mass \(m\) and \(3\text{ }m\). Find the ratio of their respective De Broglie wavelength?
stemOverrides.21: A gas has \(C_{P}-C_{V}=R\) at temperature \(T = P\) and \(C_{P}-C_{V}= 1.1R\) at temperature \(T = Q\). Then
